summary: How the blood carries oxygen and carbon dioxide, what shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve, and how to read a blood gas when breathing is the problem. Exam cases turn on O2 content math, carbon monoxide and methemoglobin traps, and judging whether renal compensation is the expected amount.

points: CaO2 = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2), in mL O2 per dL of blood.
Normal: Hb 15 g/dL, SaO2 0.98, PaO2 95 mmHg gives about 20 mL O2/dL; dissolved O2 adds only about 0.3 of that.
PaO2 is the pressure of dissolved O2; it sets SaO2 but says nothing about how much hemoglobin there is.
Anemia: PaO2 and SaO2 normal, content low (Hb 7.5 g/dL halves content to about 10 mL/dL).
Polycythemia: PaO2 and SaO2 normal, content high.
O2 delivery = cardiac output x CaO2, so low content can be partly offset by a higher cardiac output.
notes.why: Almost all arterial O2 rides on hemoglobin, so content depends on how much hemoglobin there is and how full it is, while dissolved O2 adds very little. PaO2 reflects gas exchange across the alveolar membrane and sets the percent saturation, but it cannot tell how much hemoglobin is present. This is why anemia lowers content and delivery with a normal PaO2 and SaO2, and why the body compensates by raising cardiac output and extracting more O2 in the tissues.

points: Sigmoid shape comes from cooperative binding: each O2 that binds makes the next bind more easily.
T (tense) state is deoxyhemoglobin with low O2 affinity; R (relaxed) state is oxyhemoglobin with high affinity.
P50 (PO2 at 50 percent saturation) is about 27 mmHg; a right shift raises P50, a left shift lowers it.
Right shift (easier unloading): more H+ (lower pH), more CO2, higher temperature, more 2,3-BPG, exercise.
Left shift (tighter binding): fetal hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, methemoglobin, alkalosis, low temperature, low 2,3-BPG.
The flat top keeps saturation near 90 percent until PaO2 drops below about 60 mmHg; the steep part sits at tissue PO2 levels.
notes.why: Hemoglobin is a tetramer whose four subunits change shape together. When O2 binds one heme, the iron moves into the plane of the porphyrin ring and pulls the molecule from the T state toward the R state, which raises affinity at the remaining hemes and gives the sigmoid shape. H+, CO2, and 2,3-BPG stabilize the T state, so they shift the curve right and release O2. The plateau protects loading in the lungs when alveolar PO2 falls, and the steep middle lets a small drop in tissue PO2 release a large amount of O2.

points: About 70 percent travels as bicarbonate, about 20 to 25 percent as carbaminohemoglobin, and about 5 to 10 percent dissolved.
In red cells, carbonic anhydrase makes CO2 + H2O into H2CO3, which splits into H+ and HCO3-.
HCO3- leaves the red cell in exchange for Cl- through band 3 (the chloride shift); the reverse happens in the lungs.
H+ is buffered by deoxyhemoglobin, which is a better buffer than oxyhemoglobin.
notes.why: CO2 diffuses into red cells, where carbonic anhydrase hydrates it within milliseconds, so most CO2 ends up in plasma as bicarbonate after the chloride shift. Deoxyhemoglobin buffers the H+ that is released, which keeps the reaction moving forward and limits the fall in venous pH. Carbamino compounds form on the terminal amino groups of the globin chains, and deoxyhemoglobin forms them more readily. In the lungs every step runs in reverse, regenerating CO2 that is exhaled.

points: Bohr effect (tissues): high CO2 and H+ lower hemoglobin O2 affinity, so O2 unloads where metabolism is high.
Haldane effect (lungs): oxygenation of hemoglobin lowers its affinity for CO2 and H+, so CO2 is released into the alveoli.
In tissues the two work together: unloading O2 makes deoxyhemoglobin, which picks up more CO2 and H+.
notes.why: Both effects come from one linkage: O2 binding and H+ or CO2 binding favor opposite conformations of hemoglobin. In active tissue, H+ and CO2 stabilize the T state and push O2 off (Bohr effect). In the lungs, O2 loading shifts hemoglobin to the R state, which releases bound H+ and carbamino CO2; that H+ combines with HCO3- to form CO2 for exhalation (Haldane effect). So each gas helps unload the other exactly where it needs to leave.

points: CO binds hemoglobin with about 200 times the affinity of O2, takes up binding sites, and shifts the curve left.
In CO poisoning PaO2 is normal (dissolved O2 is unaffected), true SaO2 and content are low, and standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal.
Methemoglobin has ferric (Fe3+) iron that cannot carry O2, and it left-shifts the remaining ferrous hemes.
Methemoglobinemia gives chocolate-colored blood and cyanosis that does not improve with O2; pulse oximetry tends to read about 85 percent.
Common causes of methemoglobinemia: nitrites, dapsone, benzocaine and other topical anesthetics.
Co-oximetry measures carboxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin directly and is the test that settles both.
notes.why: Both disorders lower O2 content while PaO2 stays normal, because they alter hemoglobin and leave alveolar gas exchange untouched. CO occupies heme sites and locks the remaining hemes in a high-affinity state, so less O2 is carried and what is carried unloads poorly in tissues. Oxidizing drugs convert ferrous iron to ferric iron, which cannot bind O2 and raises the affinity of the other hemes in the same tetramer. Standard pulse oximeters read only two wavelengths and cannot identify these abnormal hemoglobins, which is why co-oximetry is needed.

points: Normal: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mmHg, HCO3- 22 to 26 mEq/L.
Respiratory acidosis (hypoventilation): HCO3- rises about 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PaCO2 acutely and 3 to 4 mEq/L chronically.
Respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation): HCO3- falls about 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg acutely and 4 to 5 mEq/L chronically.
Renal compensation takes 3 to 5 days, which is why acute and chronic values differ.
If the measured HCO3- is clearly off the expected value, a second (metabolic) disorder is present.
notes.why: PaCO2 is set by alveolar ventilation, so hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers pH through the CO2 and bicarbonate equilibrium. The small acute rise in HCO3- comes from buffering by hemoglobin and other intracellular proteins. The larger chronic change appears over 3 to 5 days as the kidney increases H+ secretion and ammonium excretion and adds new bicarbonate to the blood, or does the reverse in alkalosis. Comparing measured HCO3- with the expected value tells you whether a separate metabolic disorder is also present.

tricks.label: Pressure, saturation, content
tricks.text: Ask three separate questions: Is PaO2 low (lungs)? Is SaO2 low (lungs or abnormal hemoglobin)? Is content low (any of these, or too little hemoglobin)? Anemia only fails the third.

tricks.label: Which gas pushes which
tricks.text: Bohr: CO2 and H+ push O2 off hemoglobin in the tissues. Haldane: O2 pushes CO2 and H+ off hemoglobin in the lungs.

highYield: Anemia lowers O2 content with a normal PaO2 and normal SaO2.
CO poisoning: normal PaO2, falsely normal pulse oximetry, low true saturation, left-shifted curve.
Chocolate-colored blood with cyanosis that does not respond to O2 means methemoglobinemia.
Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its curve sits to the left of adult hemoglobin.
About 70 percent of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate made by red cell carbonic anhydrase.
The chloride shift swaps HCO3- for Cl- through band 3, so venous red cells hold more chloride.
Chronic respiratory acidosis raises HCO3- 3 to 4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PaCO2; acute raises it only about 1.
pitfalls: PaO2 measures dissolved O2, so it stays normal in anemia, CO poisoning, and methemoglobinemia.
CO and methemoglobin both shift the curve left; they do not make the remaining hemoglobin release O2 more easily.
Bohr and Haldane are easy to swap: Bohr changes O2 binding, Haldane changes CO2 binding.
A PaCO2 of 60 mmHg with HCO3- of 20 mEq/L is not compensation; HCO3- should be up, so a metabolic acidosis is also present.

summary: The molecules that keep the lung working: surfactant, elastin, mucus, the antiprotease shield, and the antioxidant enzymes, plus the vitamins that support them. Questions link a biochemical failure to a lung disease, such as elastase winning over alpha-1 antitrypsin in emphysema or delayed surfactant in infants of diabetic mothers.

points: Made by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar bodies.
Main lipid is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, a lecithin); phosphatidylglycerol is a smaller but important part.
Surfactant proteins: SP-B and SP-C (hydrophobic) spread the film; SP-A and SP-D are collectins that also act as opsonins.
Lowers surface tension most in small alveoli, keeping them open at end expiration.
Fetal cortisol and thyroid hormone increase synthesis, which is why antenatal corticosteroids speed lung maturity.
Fetal hyperinsulinemia (maternal diabetes) slows synthesis, so these infants get respiratory distress at a later gestational age.
Maturity markers in amniotic fluid: lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio above 2.0 and phosphatidylglycerol present.
notes.why: Surface tension in a curved alveolus creates a collapsing pressure equal to 2T/r (law of Laplace), so without surfactant small alveoli would empty into larger ones. DPPC packs tightly as the film is compressed during expiration, so surface tension falls most as the alveolus shrinks, which keeps alveoli of different sizes stable. Fetal glucocorticoids induce type II cell maturation and the enzymes of phosphatidylcholine synthesis, while fetal insulin antagonizes this effect, which explains delayed lung maturity in infants of diabetic mothers.

points: Neutrophil elastase can digest alveolar wall elastin; alpha-1 antitrypsin (a serpin made in the liver) inhibits it.
Cigarette smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages, which release elastase and matrix metalloproteinases.
Oxidants in smoke oxidize a methionine in the reactive site of alpha-1 antitrypsin and inactivate it.
More protease plus less antiprotease tips the balance toward alveolar wall destruction (emphysema).
notes.why: Alveolar wall elastin stays intact because alpha-1 antitrypsin traps neutrophil elastase in an irreversible complex. Smoking upsets this balance from both sides: it recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase, and its oxidants inactivate the antitrypsin that should neutralize it. Unopposed elastase destroys alveolar septa, which merges airspaces and removes the radial traction that holds small airways open, producing emphysema with air trapping.

points: Elastin is rich in glycine, proline, and lysine; desmosine cross-links let it stretch and recoil.
Lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, makes these cross-links (and collagen cross-links).
Elastin loss in emphysema raises compliance and lowers recoil, so air is trapped.
Collagen deposition in fibrosis lowers compliance and raises recoil, so lung volumes shrink.
notes.why: Lung recoil comes from alveolar surface tension and from elastic fibers. Lysyl oxidase uses copper to oxidize lysine side chains into reactive aldehydes, which condense into desmosine cross-links that let elastin stretch and snap back. Losing elastin makes the lung floppy (high compliance) with weak recoil, so airways collapse during expiration and air is trapped. Depositing stiff collagen does the opposite, raising recoil and lowering lung volumes, which is the restrictive pattern.

points: Retinoic acid keeps respiratory epithelium differentiated as ciliated and mucus-secreting cells.
Vitamin A deficiency causes squamous (keratinizing) metaplasia, loss of cilia and goblet cells, and more respiratory infections.
Cystic fibrosis blocks pancreatic enzyme release, fats are poorly absorbed, and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K run low.
Results: night blindness (A), rickets or osteomalacia (D), hemolysis and neuropathy (E), bleeding (K).
notes.why: Retinoic acid acts through nuclear retinoic acid receptors that control the genes for airway epithelial differentiation. Without it, the lining shifts to keratinizing squamous epithelium that lacks cilia and goblet cells, so the mucociliary escalator fails and infections rise. In cystic fibrosis, thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts and lipase does not reach the gut, and because fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed in micelles with dietary fat, all four become deficient.

points: High inspired O2 and cigarette smoke generate superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals.
These damage membrane lipids, proteins, and DNA in alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium.
Superoxide dismutase turns superoxide into hydrogen peroxide; catalase turns hydrogen peroxide into water and O2.
Glutathione peroxidase uses selenium and reduced glutathione to clear peroxides; NADPH regenerates glutathione.
Prolonged high FiO2 causes diffuse alveolar damage in adults and adds to bronchopulmonary dysplasia in neonates.
notes.why: Reactive oxygen species form when O2 accepts single electrons, and their production rises with high FiO2 and with the oxidants in smoke. Cells clear them with a sequence of enzymes: superoxide dismutase, then catalase or glutathione peroxidase, with NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway regenerating reduced glutathione through glutathione reductase. When production outpaces this system, lipid peroxidation and protein damage injure alveolar epithelium and endothelium, causing leak and diffuse alveolar damage.

points: Mucins are large glycoproteins with heavy O-linked glycosylation on serine and threonine, added in the Golgi.
Secreted by goblet cells in the epithelium and by submucosal glands.
Chronic bronchitis: submucosal gland hyperplasia (Reid index above 0.4) and goblet cell increase make excess mucus.
Cystic fibrosis: too little water in the airway surface liquid makes mucus thick and hard for cilia to move.
notes.why: Mucins form a gel because their dense O-linked sugar chains bind large amounts of water, so the hydration of the airway surface liquid decides how easily cilia can move them. Chronic irritation from smoke enlarges submucosal glands and expands goblet cells, which increases mucus volume. In cystic fibrosis the mucus is short on water: without CFTR chloride secretion and with excess ENaC sodium absorption, the periciliary layer collapses and mucus becomes thick and sticky.

summary: The single-gene lung diseases (cystic fibrosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, primary ciliary dyskinesia) and the cell cycle genes that tobacco damages in lung cancer. Exam questions ask you to connect the mutation to the protein defect and then to the organ findings.

points: Autosomal recessive; CFTR gene on chromosome 7; carrier frequency about 1 in 25 in people of Northern European descent.
CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride channel in the ABC transporter family; it also restrains sodium uptake through ENaC.
F508 deletion (the most common allele) makes a misfolded protein that is held in the ER, ubiquitinated, and destroyed by the proteasome.
Airways: less chloride secretion and more sodium absorption pull water out, leaving thick, dehydrated mucus.
Sweat glands: chloride cannot be reabsorbed, so sweat chloride is high (60 mmol/L or more is diagnostic).
Other findings: meconium ileus, pancreatic insufficiency, male infertility from absent vas deferens, recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas infections.
notes.why: CFTR opens when protein kinase A phosphorylates its regulatory domain and ATP binds its nucleotide-binding domains, letting chloride (and bicarbonate) flow onto epithelial surfaces. The F508 deletion disrupts folding, so ER quality control tags the protein with ubiquitin for proteasomal destruction and little reaches the membrane. In airways, lost chloride secretion plus unchecked ENaC sodium absorption dehydrates the surface liquid. In the sweat duct CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride, so its loss leaves sweat salty.

points: SERPINA1 gene on chromosome 14; alleles are codominant (PiMM normal, PiMZ intermediate, PiZZ severe).
The Z protein misfolds and polymerizes in the hepatocyte ER, so little reaches the blood.
Lung: unopposed elastase causes panacinar emphysema, worst in the lower lobes, often before age 45 in smokers.
Liver: retained protein injures hepatocytes and causes hepatitis and cirrhosis.
Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes.
notes.why: The Z allele (a single glutamate to lysine substitution) lets the protein misfold and polymerize in the hepatocyte ER, which causes two separate problems. Too little antitrypsin reaches the lung, so neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls throughout the acinus, giving panacinar emphysema. The retained polymers injure hepatocytes from within, causing hepatitis and cirrhosis, and appear as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules. Because alleles are codominant, each one contributes its own protein, so PiMZ carriers have intermediate serum levels.

points: Autosomal recessive defects of dynein arms make cilia immotile or poorly beating.
Mucociliary clearance fails: chronic sinusitis, otitis media, recurrent pneumonia, bronchiectasis.
Sperm flagella share the same axoneme, so men are infertile; women have reduced fertility and more ectopic pregnancy.
Embryonic nodal cilia set left-right orientation; without them sidedness is random, so about half have situs inversus.
Kartagener syndrome is the triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis.
notes.why: Motile cilia have a 9+2 axoneme in which dynein arms use ATP to slide the outer microtubule doublets past each other and bend the cilium. Without dynein arms, mucus pools in the sinuses, middle ears, and bronchi, and repeated infection and inflammation destroy bronchial walls into bronchiectasis. Sperm flagella use the same motor, so sperm are immotile. In the embryo, rotating nodal cilia create a leftward fluid flow that sets left-right asymmetry, so without them organ position is decided by chance.

points: Rb binds E2F and blocks the G1 to S transition; cyclin D with CDK4 and CDK6 phosphorylates Rb to release E2F.
p53 senses DNA damage and induces p21, which inhibits CDKs and holds the cell in G1 for repair or apoptosis.
Benzo[a]pyrene is activated by cytochrome P450 to a diol epoxide that binds guanine and forms DNA adducts.
Unrepaired adducts cause G to T transversions, including in TP53 hot spots, which removes the G1 brake.
notes.why: The G1 checkpoint lets a cell repair DNA before copying it. Rb holds E2F inactive until cyclin D with CDK4 and CDK6 phosphorylates it, and p53 can stop this by inducing p21, a CDK inhibitor that keeps Rb unphosphorylated. Tobacco carcinogens such as benzo[a]pyrene become DNA-reactive only after P450 activation, and their guanine adducts cause G to T transversions in TP53. Losing p53 removes the damage checkpoint, so mutations pile up with each division.

points: Adenocarcinoma: activating EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements (EML4-ALK), and KRAS mutations.
EGFR mutations are most common in nonsmokers, women, and people of East Asian ancestry.
KRAS mutations are more common in smokers; KRAS and EGFR mutations rarely occur in the same tumor.
Small cell carcinoma: loss of TP53 and RB1 in nearly all tumors.
EGFR and ALK changes matter because targeted kinase inhibitors exist for them.
notes.why: A driver mutation gives the tumor a growth signal it comes to depend on. Mutant EGFR and the EML4-ALK fusion are tyrosine kinases that signal without ligand through the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways, while mutant KRAS stays locked in its active GTP-bound state further down the same pathway. Because these changes activate one pathway, a tumor gains little from carrying two of them, which is one reason they rarely occur together. Small cell carcinoma instead loses the RB1 and TP53 brakes on the cell cycle.

tricks.text: Clear mucus, move sperm, and set left from right in the embryo. Lose dynein and all three fail: bronchiectasis, infertility, and situs inversus.

tricks.text: Small cell carcinoma knocks out both G1 brakes, TP53 and RB1, which fits its fast growth.

summary: Why the body needs oxygen at all: O2 is the last electron acceptor that lets mitochondria make most ATP. This unit covers what happens when O2 delivery or use fails (lactic acidosis, cyanide and CO), the respiratory quotient, 2,3-BPG, and the energy cost of breathing in emphysema.

points: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) passes electrons to O2, making water.
Electron flow pumps protons out of the matrix; ATP synthase uses that gradient to make ATP.
Full oxidation of glucose yields about 30 to 32 ATP; glycolysis alone yields 2.
Without O2, NADH builds up and the electron transport chain stops.
Lactate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into lactate to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.
Result: lactic acidosis, an anion gap metabolic acidosis (lactate normally below about 2 mmol/L).
notes.why: O2 is the terminal electron acceptor, so it keeps electrons flowing from NADH and FADH2 through the chain to complex IV. When O2 is lacking, the chain backs up, proton pumping stops, ATP synthase slows, and NADH cannot be reoxidized to NAD+. Glycolysis needs NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step, so cells regenerate it by reducing pyruvate to lactate. The extra lactate and H+ produce an anion gap metabolic acidosis.

points: Smoke from burning plastics, foam, wool, and silk releases hydrogen cyanide; any fire releases CO.
Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome a3 in complex IV and stops O2 use.
CO also binds complex IV in addition to its effect on hemoglobin.
PaO2 stays normal because O2 still reaches the blood; cells cannot use it, so lactate rises.
In cyanide poisoning tissues extract little O2, so venous O2 saturation is high and venous blood looks bright red.
Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin; sodium thiosulfate helps rhodanese convert cyanide to thiocyanate.
notes.why: Cyanide stops complex IV, so cells cannot use O2 even though blood carries a normal amount; CO adds the same block to its main effect on hemoglobin. O2 still diffuses into the blood, which is why PaO2 stays normal, and in cyanide poisoning the unused O2 returns in venous blood and raises venous saturation. Because ATP falls, cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis and lactate rises. The antidotes give cyanide another target: hydroxocobalamin binds it directly, and thiosulfate supplies sulfur so rhodanese can form thiocyanate for renal excretion.

points: RQ = CO2 produced divided by O2 consumed.
Carbohydrate 1.0 (glucose + 6 O2 makes 6 CO2), fat about 0.7, protein about 0.8; a mixed diet is about 0.8.
Example: VCO2 200 mL/min and VO2 250 mL/min gives RQ 0.8.
Heavy carbohydrate feeding raises CO2 production, and RQ above 1.0 means net fat synthesis.
More CO2 means more ventilation needed, a problem for patients with COPD or those weaning from a ventilator.
notes.why: RQ reflects how oxidized a fuel already is. Carbohydrate carries enough oxygen in its own structure that each O2 consumed yields one CO2, while fat is highly reduced, so much of the O2 goes to forming water and RQ is about 0.7. When excess carbohydrate is converted to fat, an oxygen-rich substrate becomes an oxygen-poor product, so CO2 is released without matching O2 use and RQ exceeds 1.0. Because PaCO2 depends on CO2 production divided by alveolar ventilation, a larger CO2 load requires more ventilation to hold PaCO2 steady.

points: Made in red cells by a side path of glycolysis: bisphosphoglycerate mutase converts 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG.
The shunt skips the phosphoglycerate kinase step, so the red cell gives up one ATP for each molecule routed through it.
2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin, stabilizes the T state, and shifts the curve right.
High altitude: hypoxia and respiratory alkalosis stimulate glycolysis, raising 2,3-BPG within hours to days.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency backs up glycolytic intermediates, raising 2,3-BPG and improving O2 unloading despite anemia.
Hexokinase deficiency and stored blood lower 2,3-BPG and shift the curve left.
notes.why: 2,3-BPG carries strong negative charges that fit the positively charged central cavity between the beta chains of deoxyhemoglobin, holding it in the T state and lowering O2 affinity. Its level depends on glycolytic flux through the red cell, so a block below the shunt (pyruvate kinase deficiency) raises it, while a block above it (hexokinase deficiency) lowers it. Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly because its gamma chains lack a positively charged histidine found in beta chains, which explains its higher O2 affinity.

points: Normally breathing uses only a few percent of total O2 consumption.
In severe emphysema, air trapping and a flattened diaphragm make each breath cost far more energy.
Resting energy expenditure rises while dyspnea and early fullness cut food intake.
Result: weight loss and muscle wasting, and a low body mass index predicts worse survival.
notes.why: Work of breathing rises when muscles must move air through collapsing airways, and hyperinflation leaves the diaphragm short and flat, where it generates force inefficiently. The O2 cost of breathing therefore climbs and takes a much larger share of resting energy use. With intake limited by dyspnea, the energy gap is filled by breaking down fat and muscle, including respiratory muscle, which further weakens ventilation.

summary: How the lung defends itself and how immune responses cause lung disease. Exam questions link a disease to its hypersensitivity type and key cytokine: IgE and Th2 in asthma, Th1 and TNF-alpha in granulomas, anti-GBM antibodies in Goodpasture syndrome, and conjugate vaccines that recruit T cell help.

points: Nose traps large particles (above about 10 micrometers); smaller ones stick to airway mucus and ride the mucociliary escalator up to be coughed or swallowed.
Secretory IgA (a dimer with J chain and secretory component) blocks microbe attachment on mucosa.
Alveolar macrophages clear microbes and particles small enough to reach the alveoli (about 1 to 5 micrometers).
Surfactant proteins A and D bind microbes and act as opsonins for macrophages.
Smoking paralyzes cilia and impairs macrophages; alcohol blunts cough and gag reflexes and raises aspiration risk; ciliary defects stop clearance.
notes.why: Defenses are layered by particle size and depth in the airway. Large particles impact in the nose, smaller ones land on mucus that coordinated ciliary beating carries upward, and secretory IgA keeps microbes from attaching to the epithelium. Particles that reach the alveoli meet macrophages, helped by SP-A and SP-D, which bind microbial surface sugars and opsonize them. Smoking, alcohol, and ciliary defects each remove one of these layers, which is why each raises pneumonia risk.

points: Dendritic cells present allergen and drive Th2 cells.
IL-4 drives B cell class switching to IgE; IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils; IL-13 drives mucus production and airway hyperreactivity.
IgE coats mast cells through FcεRI; re-exposure cross-links IgE and triggers degranulation.
Early phase (minutes): histamine, prostaglandin D2, and leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 cause bronchoconstriction, mucus, and leak.
Late phase (about 4 to 8 hours): eosinophils and Th2 cells arrive; major basic protein injures epithelium; sputum may show Charcot-Leyden crystals.
notes.why: Allergic asthma is driven by Th2 cells. Dendritic cells present allergen to naive CD4 T cells in the presence of IL-4, and the resulting Th2 cytokines each drive one feature: IL-4 switches B cells to IgE, IL-5 produces and activates eosinophils, and IL-13 drives goblet cell mucus and airway hyperresponsiveness. Preformed and newly made mast cell mediators cause the early response within minutes, while recruited eosinophils and T cells cause the late phase and the epithelial damage that keeps inflammation going.

points: Macrophages make IL-12, which drives Th1 cells.
Th1 cells make IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages into epithelioid cells and giant cells.
TNF-alpha holds the granuloma together.
TNF-alpha blockers can let latent tuberculosis reactivate, so patients are screened first.
Tuberculosis granulomas caseate; sarcoidosis granulomas do not.
notes.why: A granuloma walls off an antigen that macrophages cannot destroy. Macrophage IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation, Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, and the activated macrophages become epithelioid cells that can fuse into multinucleated giant cells. TNF-alpha from macrophages keeps this structure organized, which is why blocking TNF can break down granulomas that contain dormant mycobacteria. Caseous necrosis in the center reflects the intense cell-mediated response to mycobacterial antigens.

points: Repeated inhalation of organic antigens: thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay (farmer lung), bird proteins.
Type III (precipitating IgG immune complexes) and type IV (T cell) reactions in the interstitium and small airways.
Histology: lymphocytic interstitial infiltrate with poorly formed noncaseating granulomas.
Acute episodes bring fever, cough, and dyspnea 4 to 6 hours after exposure; chronic exposure causes fibrosis.
Unlike asthma: no IgE, no eosinophilia, restrictive pattern, reduced DLCO.
notes.why: Organic antigens such as actinomycete spores are small enough to reach the terminal bronchioles and alveoli, where repeated exposure induces precipitating IgG. Immune complexes form in the alveolar walls, activate complement, and recruit neutrophils over several hours, which explains the 4 to 6 hour delay of acute episodes. Continued exposure shifts the reaction toward T cell inflammation with poorly formed granulomas and eventually fibrosis. Because the injury is in the alveolar walls and IgE plays no part, the pattern is restrictive with a low DLCO.

points: Goodpasture syndrome: type II hypersensitivity; IgG against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.
Goodpasture causes pulmonary hemorrhage (hemoptysis) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with linear IgG on immunofluorescence.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA), necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.
It hits the upper airway (sinusitis, nasal ulcers, saddle nose), lungs (cavitating nodules), and kidneys (pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis).
notes.why: Goodpasture antibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, which is present in both glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. The antibody binds evenly along the membrane, giving linear IgG staining, and complement activation and neutrophils damage capillaries in both organs. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis works differently: PR3-ANCA activates primed neutrophils that injure small vessel walls, so the kidney shows few or no immune deposits (pauci-immune).

points: Toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus) are inactivated toxins that induce neutralizing IgG antitoxin.
Acellular pertussis vaccine contains pertussis toxoid plus adhesins such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin.
Plain polysaccharides are T cell independent: mostly IgM, little memory, weak response under age 2.
Conjugate vaccines (Hib, pneumococcal) link polysaccharide to a protein so B cells present carrier peptides to helper T cells.
T cell help gives class switching to IgG, affinity maturation, memory, and protection in infants.
notes.why: Toxoids are toxins chemically inactivated so they no longer cause disease while keeping their antigenic epitopes, so the IgG they induce neutralizes the real toxin. Polysaccharides have repeating epitopes that cross-link B cell receptors without T cell help, which gives short-lived IgM and poor responses in children under 2. Linking the polysaccharide to a protein lets the polysaccharide-specific B cell take in the carrier and present its peptides on MHC class II. Helper T cells then supply CD40 ligand and cytokines for class switching, affinity maturation, and memory.

points: Tumors lower MHC class I to hide from CD8 T cells.
Tumors express PD-L1, which binds PD-1 on T cells and switches them off; anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 drugs block this.
Small cell carcinoma shares antigens with neurons, so antibodies against the tumor also hit nerves.
Anti-Hu: paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis and sensory neuronopathy.
Anti-voltage-gated calcium channel: Lambert-Eaton syndrome, proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort.
notes.why: CD8 T cells recognize tumor peptides on MHC class I, so tumors that reduce class I expression escape them. PD-L1 on tumor cells engages PD-1, an inhibitory receptor on activated T cells that dampens their signaling, and checkpoint inhibitor drugs release this brake. Small cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor that expresses neuronal proteins, so antibodies raised against the tumor cross-react with neurons or with presynaptic calcium channels, causing paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes.

summary: The bacteria, viruses, and fungi behind lung infections, with the lab features and virulence factors that identify each. Exam questions pair a host or exposure clue with an organism, then ask about its toxin, capsule, culture needs, or how it evades immunity.

points: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci; alpha-hemolytic (partial, green).
Optochin sensitive and bile soluble, which separates it from viridans streptococci.
Polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor; IgA protease and pneumolysin add to it.
Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia and of lobar pneumonia; rust-colored sputum.
Asplenia raises risk of severe infection with encapsulated organisms like this one.
notes.why: The polysaccharide capsule blocks complement deposition and phagocytosis, which is why opsonizing antibody and the spleen are central to defense against it. IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA so the organism can colonize the nasopharynx, and pneumolysin, a pore-forming toxin, damages epithelium and drives inflammation as alveoli fill with exudate. Optochin sensitivity and bile solubility (bile salts activate the organism's autolysin) are the lab traits that separate it from viridans streptococci.

points: Haemophilus influenzae: small coccobacillus, needs factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD+), grows on chocolate agar.
H. influenzae type b capsule causes invasive disease; nontypeable strains cause otitis, sinusitis, and COPD flares.
Klebsiella pneumoniae: lactose-fermenting rod with a thick mucoid capsule; alcoholics and aspiration; currant jelly sputum, abscesses.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting aerobic rod; blue-green pigment; cystic fibrosis and ventilated patients.
Legionella pneumophila: stains poorly with Gram stain; grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with iron and cysteine.
Legionella spreads from contaminated water (cooling towers, plumbing), not person to person; hyponatremia and diarrhea are clues; urine antigen test.
notes.why: The lab and clinical clues for each organism follow from its biology. H. influenzae cannot make heme (factor X) or NAD+ (factor V), so it needs chocolate agar, and its type b capsule lets it survive in the blood and invade. Klebsiella's thick capsule resists phagocytosis, and aspiration of colonized oral secretions in alcoholics explains its necrotizing pneumonia. Pseudomonas thrives in moist settings and in the thick mucus of cystic fibrosis, while Legionella multiplies inside amoebae in water systems and needs added iron and cysteine to grow in culture.

points: Corynebacterium diphtheriae: gram-positive club-shaped rods; the toxin gene comes from a prophage (lysogenic conversion).
Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 and stops protein synthesis, killing cells.
Clinical result: gray pseudomembrane in the pharynx, bull neck, myocarditis, and cranial nerve palsies.
Bordetella pertussis: gram-negative coccobacillus; pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi, so Gi cannot inhibit adenylyl cyclase and cAMP rises.
Clinical result: catarrhal stage, then paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting, plus marked lymphocytosis.
notes.why: Both toxins have a binding part that gets them into cells and an active part that transfers ADP-ribose from NAD+ to a host protein. Diphtheria toxin inactivates elongation factor 2, so translation stops and cells die, which forms the pseudomembrane locally and damages heart and nerves when toxin circulates. Pertussis toxin modifies Gi so it can no longer inhibit adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP rises and impairs phagocyte function. Blocking Gi-coupled chemokine signaling also keeps lymphocytes from leaving the blood, which produces the marked lymphocytosis.

points: Acid-fast because of mycolic acids in a waxy cell wall; obligate aerobe; slow growing.
Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) activates macrophages and drives TNF-alpha release and granulomas.
Sulfatides help block phagosome and lysosome fusion, so the organism survives inside macrophages.
Spread by airborne droplet nuclei small enough to reach the alveoli.
Primary infection: Ghon focus in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe; reactivation favors the apices.
notes.why: Mycolic acids make the wall waxy and resistant to decolorization by acid alcohol, which is the basis of acid-fast staining. Inside macrophages the organism blocks phagolysosome fusion and survives until Th1 cells activate those macrophages with IFN-gamma, and cord factor drives the TNF-alpha release that organizes granulomas. Primary infection lands in the well-ventilated middle lung zones, while reactivation favors the apices, where the high PO2 suits this obligate aerobe.

points: Influenza: orthomyxovirus with 8 segments of negative-sense RNA; hemagglutinin binds sialic acid, neuraminidase releases new virions.
Antigenic drift (point mutations) causes yearly epidemics; antigenic shift (segment reassortment, influenza A) causes pandemics.
Influenza is often followed by bacterial pneumonia from Staphylococcus aureus, S. pneumoniae, or H. influenzae.
Respiratory syncytial virus: nonsegmented negative-sense RNA pneumovirus (formerly grouped with paramyxoviruses).
RSV F protein fuses cells into syncytia; RSV is the top cause of bronchiolitis in infants.
Coronaviruses: enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA; SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds ACE2.
notes.why: Influenza hemagglutinin binds sialic acid to enter cells, and neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release new virions. The viral RNA polymerase makes frequent errors, producing point mutations (drift), and the segmented genome lets two influenza A strains swap segments in one cell (shift). Virus kills ciliated epithelium and strips away mucociliary clearance, opening the airway to bacterial superinfection. RSV F protein fuses infected cells with their neighbors into syncytia, and infants' narrow bronchioles plug easily with the resulting debris and mucus.

points: Dimorphic fungi grow as molds at room temperature and as yeasts (or spherules) at body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F).
Histoplasma: Ohio and Mississippi river valleys, bird and bat droppings; small yeasts inside macrophages.
Blastomyces: Great Lakes and Ohio and Mississippi basins; large yeast with a thick wall and broad-based bud; skin and bone spread.
Coccidioides: southwestern United States desert dust; spherules filled with endospores; erythema nodosum and arthralgias.
Aspergillus: septate hyphae branching at acute angles (about 45 degrees); invasive disease with neutropenia.
Pneumocystis jirovecii: cysts on methenamine silver stain; diffuse interstitial pneumonia when CD4 count is below 200 cells/mm3.
notes.why: Dimorphism is a temperature switch: environmental molds release spores that are inhaled, and at body temperature the fungus converts to its tissue form. Histoplasma yeasts survive inside macrophages, so infection spreads with them through the reticuloendothelial system, while Blastomyces spreads through the blood to skin and bone. Aspergillus and Pneumocystis are opportunists that cause invasive disease mainly when the defenses that normally control them are missing, neutrophils for Aspergillus and CD4 T cells for Pneumocystis.

summary: Restrictive lung diseases keep the lungs from filling: surfactant failure in newborns, diffuse alveolar damage in ARDS, scarring in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and the pneumoconioses, and granulomas in sarcoidosis. Exam questions ask you to match an exposure, histology, or lab pattern to the disease and to separate lung-tissue causes from chest wall and muscle causes.

points: Surfactant deficiency; risk rises with prematurity, maternal diabetes, cesarean delivery without labor, and male sex.
High surface tension collapses alveoli at end expiration (atelectasis), causing shunt, hypoxemia, and hyaline membranes (fibrin and dead cells).
Signs within hours of birth: tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions; ground-glass X-ray with air bronchograms.
Hypoxemia keeps the ductus arteriosus open (patent ductus arteriosus).
O2 and ventilation can cause bronchopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity.
notes.why: By the law of Laplace, collapsing pressure equals 2T/r, so without surfactant the smallest alveoli collapse at the end of each breath. Collapsed alveoli that are still perfused act as a right-to-left shunt, so hypoxemia responds poorly to supplemental O2. Injured epithelium and capillaries leak protein that forms hyaline membranes with necrotic cells. Hypoxemia and acidosis keep pulmonary vascular resistance high and the ductus arteriosus open, while the high O2 and pressures used in treatment injure developing lungs and retinal vessels.

points: Diffuse alveolar damage after sepsis (most common), pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, or pancreatitis.
Macrophage cytokines recruit neutrophils, which release proteases and oxidants and break the capillary and epithelial barrier.
Protein-rich fluid floods alveoli and hyaline membranes form.
Criteria: onset within 1 week, bilateral infiltrates, edema not explained by heart failure, PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less.
Example: PaO2 75 mmHg on FiO2 0.5 gives a ratio of 150 (moderate ARDS); hypoxemia responds poorly to O2 because of shunt.
notes.why: The common pathway is injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier, reached through the airway (pneumonia, aspiration) or the blood (sepsis, pancreatitis). Activated macrophages release IL-1, IL-8, and TNF, and recruited neutrophils release proteases and reactive oxygen species that damage endothelium and type I pneumocytes. Protein-rich fluid floods alveoli, inactivates surfactant, and forms hyaline membranes. Because flooded alveoli are still perfused, the hypoxemia behaves as shunt and responds poorly to O2.

points: Older adults, more often men and smokers; repeated alveolar epithelial injury with abnormal repair.
TGF-beta drives fibroblasts and myofibroblasts to lay down collagen.
Usual interstitial pneumonia pattern: patchy subpleural and basal scar of different ages, fibroblastic foci, and honeycomb cysts at end stage.
Dry cough, slowly worsening dyspnea, fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles, clubbing.
Spirometry: low FVC and TLC, FEV1/FVC normal or high; DLCO reduced.
notes.why: The current model is repeated microinjury to alveolar epithelium in a susceptible person, followed by abnormal repair. Injured epithelium releases TGF-beta, which activates fibroblasts and turns them into myofibroblasts that lay down collagen in fibroblastic foci. Because injury happens at different times, scars of different ages sit side by side, the hallmark of usual interstitial pneumonia. Stiff lungs shrink all volumes while extra radial traction holds airways open, so FEV1/FVC stays normal or high, and the thickened membrane lowers DLCO.

points: Coal workers: upper lobes; coal macules and nodules, sometimes progressive massive fibrosis.
Silicosis (sandblasting, quarrying, foundries): upper lobe nodules, eggshell calcified hilar nodes, and higher tuberculosis risk because silica injures macrophages.
Asbestosis (shipyards, insulation, roofing, plumbing): lower lobes, ferruginous bodies (iron-coated fibers).
Asbestos also causes calcified pleural plaques, bronchogenic carcinoma (the most common cancer), and mesothelioma.
Berylliosis (aerospace, electronics): type IV reaction with noncaseating granulomas that mimic sarcoidosis.
notes.why: Inhaled mineral particles are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, which release cytokines and growth factors that drive fibroblasts. Silica is directly toxic to macrophages: it ruptures phagolysosomes, activates the inflammasome, and kills the cell, so the particle is released and taken up again, which sustains fibrosis and weakens defense against mycobacteria. Long, thin asbestos fibers travel to the lower lobes and pleura, where an iron and protein coat turns them into ferruginous bodies. Beryllium acts as an antigen, causing a T cell granulomatous reaction.

points: Noncaseating granulomas in many organs from a Th1 response to an unknown antigen.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is the classic X-ray finding, with or without interstitial lung disease.
Serum ACE is often elevated (made by granuloma cells).
Granuloma macrophages have 1-alpha-hydroxylase, make calcitriol, and cause hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.
More common in Black women; usual onset age 20 to 40; eyes (uveitis), skin, and heart can be involved.
Lofgren syndrome: erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis (often ankles), and fever; usually resolves.
notes.why: Sarcoidosis is an exaggerated Th1 response to an unidentified antigen that produces noncaseating granulomas in lymph nodes, lungs, and other organs. Activated granuloma macrophages make ACE and also express 1-alpha-hydroxylase that escapes the normal feedback control by PTH and calcium. The calcitriol they produce raises intestinal calcium absorption, causing hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria with a suppressed PTH.

points: Intrinsic (lung tissue scar or fluid): low TLC, low DLCO, wide A-a gradient.
Extrapulmonary: obesity, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular weakness (ALS, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome).
The alveolar membrane is normal, so DLCO is usually normal; hypoventilation raises PaCO2 with a normal A-a gradient.
notes.why: Both forms shrink lung volumes, but the problem sits in different places. Intrinsic disease thickens or fills the alveolar wall, so diffusion is impaired, DLCO falls, and the A-a gradient widens. In extrapulmonary restriction the lung tissue is normal and the chest wall or respiratory muscles fail, so gas exchange is preserved; reduced ventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2 together, which keeps the A-a gradient normal.

points: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia: smokers; alveoli filled with pigmented macrophages; improves when smoking stops.
Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia: uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis (all the same age); linked to connective tissue disease.
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia: polypoid plugs of loose fibroblast tissue (Masson bodies) in small airways and alveoli; responds to steroids.
Byssinosis: cotton dust, chest tightness on the first workday of the week; bagassosis: moldy sugarcane, a hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Silo-filler disease: nitrogen dioxide from fresh silage causes pulmonary edema and later bronchiolitis obliterans.
Drug-induced fibrosis: bleomycin, amiodarone, busulfan, methotrexate (also nitrofurantoin); the drug history separates it from IPF.
notes.why: Each of these diseases has its own histologic pattern, and the pattern predicts how it behaves. Desquamative interstitial pneumonia and cryptogenic organizing pneumonia are dominated by inflammation or loose, young fibroblast tissue that can resolve, so they improve when smoking stops or with steroids. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia shows uniform, same-age changes that point to a single process such as connective tissue disease, and it carries a better prognosis than usual interstitial pneumonia. Occupational and drug exposures injure the lung directly, so the history separates them from IPF.

flows.title: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
steps: Preterm type II pneumocytes make too little surfactant
Surface tension rises and alveoli collapse at end expiration
Perfused but unventilated alveoli create shunt and hypoxemia
Repeated collapse injures epithelium; leaked fibrin and dead cells form hyaline membranes
Hypoxemia and acidosis keep the ductus arteriosus open

flows.title: ARDS pathogenesis
steps: Pneumonia, aspiration, sepsis, or trauma activates macrophages and endothelium
Cytokines (IL-1, IL-8, TNF) recruit neutrophils to the lung
Neutrophil proteases and oxidants damage endothelium and type I pneumocytes
Protein-rich fluid floods alveoli and inactivates surfactant
Hyaline membranes form, and shunt causes hypoxemia that responds poorly to O2

flows.title: Sarcoidosis and hypercalcemia
steps: A Th1 response to an unknown antigen forms noncaseating granulomas
Activated granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase
They convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without normal feedback control
Calcitriol raises intestinal calcium absorption
Hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria develop, and PTH is suppressed

tricks.label: Asbestos sits low
tricks.text: Asbestosis hits the lower lobes; coal and silica hit the upper lobes. Think of asbestos fibers sinking to the bottom.

tricks.label: Check DLCO to find the problem
tricks.text: Restriction with a low DLCO means the lung tissue is sick. Restriction with a normal DLCO means the chest wall or muscles are the problem.

tricks.label: Same age or mixed ages
tricks.text: UIP looks like scars of many ages side by side. NSIP looks like everything happened at once.

highYield: Infants of diabetic mothers get respiratory distress because fetal insulin delays surfactant.
ARDS: PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less with bilateral infiltrates not explained by heart failure.
IPF: TGF-beta driven fibrosis, UIP pattern, clubbing, restrictive spirometry, low DLCO.
Silicosis raises tuberculosis risk and shows eggshell calcification of hilar nodes.
Ferruginous bodies and pleural plaques mean asbestos exposure.
Sarcoidosis hypercalcemia comes from macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
Lofgren syndrome: erythema nodosum, hilar nodes, arthritis, fever, good prognosis.
Bleomycin and amiodarone are classic causes of drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
pitfalls: Neonatal RDS is surfactant deficiency; ARDS is diffuse alveolar damage with leak. Both show hyaline membranes.
Berylliosis granulomas look like sarcoidosis; ask about aerospace or electronics work.
Mesothelioma is the cancer most specific to asbestos, yet bronchogenic carcinoma is more common in asbestos workers.
Obesity and neuromuscular weakness cause restriction with a normal DLCO and a normal A-a gradient.
Byssinosis behaves like asthma (obstructive); bagassosis is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

dumps.p: Make a table of coal workers pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis, and berylliosis. For each, write the job, the lobe affected, the key finding, and the main complication.
l: Coal: miners, upper lobes, coal macules
Coal complication: progressive massive fibrosis
Silica: sandblasting and quarrying, upper lobes, eggshell calcified hilar nodes
Silicosis raises tuberculosis risk
Asbestos: shipyards and insulation, lower lobes, ferruginous bodies, pleural plaques
Asbestos complications: bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma
Beryllium: aerospace, noncaseating granulomas like sarcoidosis

dumps.p: Draw two alveoli side by side, one from a premature newborn with RDS and one from an adult with ARDS. Label what goes wrong in each, then list causes and complications under each drawing.
l: Newborn: low surfactant, collapsed alveolus
Newborn causes: prematurity, maternal diabetes, cesarean without labor
Adult: neutrophils damage capillary and epithelium, protein-rich fluid floods alveolus
Adult causes: sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis
Both show hyaline membranes
ARDS criterion: PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less, not explained by heart failure
Newborn complications: patent ductus, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity
Adult complication: later interstitial fibrosis
